coverage.teaching_item: Overview

review.evidence:
Overview; compared with rewritten passage at #gateway-brief: Design a gateway for a customer-support agent that survives a provider outage without customer-visible downtime, resists prompt injection and personally identifiable information (PII) leaks, spends less than $500 per day, and keeps p95 latency below three seconds. P95 means 95% of the measured requests finish within that time. The first discovery question is what counts as finishing: the first streamed token or the complete answer.

A gateway is the shared path through which model traffic passes. It screens, meters, routes and recovers each call. A customer message may trigger an agent turn with several model and tool steps. Screening only that message leaves the later paid calls outside the budget and recovery controls.

This case is for engineers preparing for Forward Deployed, solutions and applied AI interviews. It assumes familiarity with model APIs, token pricing, API gateways, retries and circuit breakers. Work through the dollar arithmetic before reading the solution, then rehearse the design and cost pivot. The target is an explainable design, not a deployed gateway. The source is a mock design built from a production and operations tutorial: its prompt, seven-point rubric and strong-answer outline supply the constraints. Pricing, latency and residency receive further worked treatment here.

coverage.teaching_item: Two gateway faces and 5–20 sub-requests

review.evidence:
Two gateway faces and 5–20 sub-requests; compared with rewritten passage at #two-faces: The edge face screens customer input and final agent output. The model face sits between every agent or evaluator call and its provider. The source playbook estimates that one user request can become 5 to 20 sub-requests. Budget enforcement at the edge alone therefore misses most of an agent's spend and leaves later failures unrecovered.

One source-reported research platform uses a shared sidecar: agents ask for a function, and configuration maps that function to a provider. When a provider changes, the team changes one mapping rather than provider code in five places. This is the shared function-to-model layer a platform can extend to further agents.

The case assumes 10,000 daily users and three turns each, one customer across several regions, and a prohibition on PII reaching an unauthorised customer or provider. coverage.teaching_item: Four testable constraints and latency measurement

review.evidence:
Four testable constraints and latency measurement; compared with rewritten passage at #requirements: Turn each requirement into a test and assign an owning component. During a single-provider outage, every customer response must be answered, labelled as degraded, or handed off. That is a useful availability test. It does not establish that all outages can produce an equivalent model answer.

The latency targets are p95 under three seconds to first token on every turn and to full answer on one-call turns. Enforce the daily $500 ledger before admission. The illustrative per-call input cap is 8,000 tokens. Reject an oversized call explicitly rather than silently truncating context.

Version the red-team suite and block release when a known attack passes through input or output checks. This is a finite regression requirement. It cannot establish zero residual injection risk. Apply PII policy to responses and logs, tag every answer with model and provider, and retain enough trace information to reconstruct guard decisions, route, tokens and cost.

Safe caching, region routing, real-path red teaming and versioned configuration make these requirements operable. The tables connect each requirement to a component, so an interview answer can name who enforces it. coverage.teaching_item: Historical unit prices and exact daily arithmetic

review.evidence:
Historical unit prices and exact daily arithmetic; compared with rewritten passage at #pricing: Use 30,000 turns a day: 10,000 users multiplied by three turns. A 30% cache hit rate removes 9,000 generation paths. Of 21,000 misses, 70% are simple one-call turns and 30% are complex five-call turns. Five calls is the low end of the source's 5 to 20 sub-request rule. Each call has 2,000 input and 250 output tokens.

At the historical illustrative small-model rates of $0.15 input and $0.60 output per million tokens, one call costs (2,000 × 0.15 + 250 × 0.60) / 1,000,000 = $0.00045. At the large-model rates of $2.50 and $10.00, the call costs $0.0075. Five such calls cost $0.0375.

Multiply those unit costs by 14,700 simple turns and 6,300 complex turns. Add $1.05 for 21,000 router classifications at $0.00005 and $1.35 for 15,000 input checks at $0.00005 plus 6,000 output checks at $0.0001. The total is $245.265, reported as about $245 or 49% of budget. Simple turns come to $6.615, shown as $6.62 in the table. Cache hits cost no generation tokens in this model, but still require gateway infrastructure and safety processing.

Without caching or routing, 30,000 five-call large-model turns cost $1,125, or 2.25 times the cap. Complex turns are 21% of all traffic and about 96% of this modelled spend. Increasing their share of misses from 30% to 40% raises daily spend to about $323. Holding all rates and proportions constant, $500 buys roughly 61,000 turns. That is a sensitivity estimate, not a capacity promise. coverage.teaching_item: Fourteen component responsibilities and failure modes

review.evidence:
Fourteen component responsibilities and failure modes; compared with rewritten passage at #architecture: The source diagrams show the same request path in several arrangements, with a versioned control plane above it. Read them as one system rather than competing designs. The control plane holds guard rules, banned phrases, routes and thresholds, prompts, provider and residency registry, budgets, pacing and red-team versions. Bad configuration must roll back atomically rather than leave half the workers on unsafe policy.

review.evidence:

A small-model guard classifies the intent of the surviving text and can recognise that rephrase, while spending money and a few hundred milliseconds.

Run checks in both directions. Mask a customer's PII before forwarding input. Validate output because a model can repeat something the customer supplied two turns earlier. A clean current input cannot prove that conversation history is safe to disclose.

Moderation applies a fixed general harm taxonomy, including harassment, hate, self-harm, sexual content and violence. Category scores determine flags. The source reports that mild rudeness such as “you are very poor ha ha” passed its moderation test. Product guardrails separately enforce support scope and system-prompt secrecy. A moderation pass does not mean a product-policy pass.

Log a reason for every block, return a safe reply and retain evidence for security review. A source-reported research platform attacks its own public endpoint through the normal auth, rate-limit and guard path. Include custom vulnerabilities for narrow policy exceptions: an apparently reasonable exception can reveal exactly the fact an attacker asks for. Both rule and LLM defences remain probabilistic. Report measured residual risk rather than invent a zero-risk promise.

coverage.teaching_item: Exact versus embedding-based semantic caching

review.evidence:
Exact versus embedding-based semantic caching; compared with rewritten passage at #safe-cache: An exact cache normalises the PII-masked query and hashes it into a lookup key. “What is Python?” and “Tell me about Python” remain different inputs. A class called SemanticCache that only hashes text still implements exact matching.

A semantic cache embeds the query into a vector and searches nearby stored vectors. A tuned similarity threshold decides whether a paraphrase can reuse an answer. A loose threshold can return mismatched or stale answers. Start with exact matching and introduce vector lookup only when observed traffic contains enough repeated paraphrases to justify its risk and operating cost.

Include tenant, user permission, document version and prompt version in the response key. Cache reusable FAQ responses, never live account answers. Changing a prompt or knowledge version deliberately invalidates prior entries. Invalidate on document, access-control list (ACL) or metadata changes. Freshness and permission checks still apply to semantic hits.

A sudden hit-rate drop is a reason to inspect keying, versioning, traffic mix and invalidation before adding capacity. Output validation precedes writes: a blocked answer must never become a future cache hit.

coverage.teaching_item: Jittered retry and three-state breaker

review.evidence:
Jittered retry and three-state breaker; compared with rewritten passage at #recovery: A retry handles a transient connection drop or provider rate limit. Exponential backoff with jitter spreads clients across time. Fixed intervals synchronise retries into a thundering herd. The source's general pattern allows three to four attempts, but interactive requests must obey a deadline instead.

The breaker wraps the retried provider call and remembers dependency health. The illustrative settings are failure_threshold=3 and cooldown_seconds=5.0. Closed admits calls. Open rejects immediately. After cooldown, half-open admits a probe. Success permits recovery. Without the probe, the breaker has no path back to healthy. Under flapping load, count failures over a sliding window and require more than one successful probe before closing.

Fallback sends work to an independent provider when retries run out or the breaker opens. Attribute every response to its actual provider and model to measure cost and quality drift. Portable prompts and tool schemas prevent a different tool-calling format from silently breaking the agent. Keep the backup warm, verify quota at full load, and distinguish provider 429 responses from your own gateway limits.

When neither provider can answer, the edge can return a labelled response seeded from safe cached context, or log a ticket for a person. The model face must return a typed error. Giving an agent a degraded prose string as if it were a real model answer can cause a refund or booking against stale information. Recovery also obeys residency and spend policy.

coverage.teaching_item: All thirteen original self-check questions and worked answers

review.evidence:
All thirteen original self-check questions and worked answers; compared with rewritten passage at #blank-page: Start from a blank page. Reproduce the four constraints, clarify both gateway faces and define the latency measurement. Price the 30,000-turn day before choosing a provider. Draw admission, recovery, validation, cache and telemetry boundaries. Then simulate a region-bound provider outage and an exhausted daily budget.

The self-checks below come from the captured source. Each answer is native page content behind a reveal. The additional blank-page simulation above is authored practice. Reading progress records reading only. Mark practice attempts separately and use the rubric to assess reasoning. Why must the gateway sit under the agent’s model calls, and not only in front of the customer’s message? The source estimates 5 to 20 sub-requests per agent turn. An edge-only gateway misses later paid calls and cannot retry or fail over them. Route every model and evaluator call through the model face, while the edge face screens customer-facing input and output. Price the day aloud. 14,700 × $0.00045 = $6.615 for simple turns. 6,300 × $0.0375 = $236.25 for five-call complex turns. Router $1.05 plus guards $1.35 gives $245.265, or about $245. Complex spend divided by total is about 96%. All rates and mix are historical illustrations. What does the naive design cost? Without cache or routing, all 30,000 turns make five large-model calls. Each turn costs 5 × $0.0075 = $0.0375. Daily cost is 30,000 × $0.0375 = $1,125, which divided by $500 is 2.25. Why does the input guard run before the cache? It blocks known injection attempts and masks PII before lookup. The key therefore uses masked text. Output validation must also pass before writing a response, preventing a blocked answer from being reused. Why is a class named SemanticCache in the source not semantic? It hashes normalised text into exact keys. The two Python paraphrases have different hashes and miss. Semantic lookup needs embeddings, a similarity search and a tuned threshold, while still enforcing permission, version and freshness boundaries. What is the difference between a per-request cap and the pacer? The cap rejects one oversized call before spending. The pacer watches the day’s accumulated spend. At 80% it tightens expensive routing, at 95% it permits the small route and complex handoff, and at 100% it permits only cache and handoff. Provider usage reconciles the ledger after each admitted call. Order the resilience chain and say what each link handles. Retry handles a transient blip with deadline-bounded jittered backoff. A breaker wraps retried calls and remembers an unhealthy provider. Fallback chooses another policy-allowed provider. Degradation supplies labelled customer help or handoff after no provider remains. The model face returns a typed failure. Why does the model face return a typed error rather than a degraded string? An agent could treat an approximate degraded reply as reliable model state and issue a refund or booking at a stale price. The typed error forces the workflow to handle failure explicitly. A human can receive labelled degradation or a ticket handoff at the edge. Sum the common-path latency. Using upper estimates, 1 ms rule guard + 10 ms cache + 400 ms router + 2,000 ms model + 1 ms validator = 2,412 ms, about 2.4 s. A 300 to 500 ms output check raises this toward 2.9 s. These stage estimates require end-to-end measurement before making a p95 claim. Why can p95 full-answer latency never be under 3 s here? Under the stated five-sequential-call assumption, complex turns take 5 to 10 s and form 21% of all turns. The fastest 79% cannot cover the 95th percentile. Agree first-token measurement for multi-step turns, or change the workflow/mix rather than promise an impossible full-answer SLO. Why can’t a typical retry schedule run on the interactive path during an outage? The waits 0.3 + 0.6 + 1.2 total 2.1 s before attempt four, excluding failed-call timeouts. Use a request deadline, retry only with sufficient remaining time, and let an open breaker skip the failed primary. Failover must still fit within that deadline. A region-bound customer’s primary provider goes down. Where does traffic go? Choose another endpoint in the same allowed region or a permitted in-network replica pool. If neither can answer, hand off. The global pool remains forbidden. Apply the same restriction to traces, cache and logs. What is the cost card’s 60-second line? Complex agent turns dominate spend at 96% of the illustrative total. Route fewer suitable turns there, cap agent steps and use a one-call workflow for common intents. Cache only safe answers.
